News.title: Total failure of UK’s electricity grid due to Iran War prepared for by government disaster planners
News.content:
GOVERNMENT disaster planners are preparing for a total failure of the UK’s electricity grid due to the Iran War, The Sun can reveal.

Officials fear a perfect storm of fuel shortages, targeted cyber attacks and public panic could spark a national power outage that would leave millions facing rolling blackouts.



The Cabinet Office is now installing £150,000 military-grade satellite phones across Government departments at key sites.



These phones — which will work even if the grid goes down — will link the Home Office to police headquarters and the Ministry of Justice.

The communication network will also be expanded to include the Department of Health and Social Care, Defra, local councils and utility firms.

Fears over emergency response capabilities and fuel supplies were discussed at a Government energy risk meeting just a few days ago.

Food and water supplies are also understood to be a major concern.



A Government spokesman told The Sun yesterday: “We have already taken action to put the interests of British people at the forefront of our response to war in the Middle East.

“Because of this, the UK is in a good position, and the public should carry on as normal.

“As is normal practice, we maintain contingency arrangements for a wide range of scenarios, however unlikely.”

News.title: Cut benefits for migrants to help bring down ballooning welfare bill, poll of Brits finds
News.content:
'CUT MIGRANT BENEFITS' Cut benefits for migrants to help bring down ballooning welfare bill, poll of Brits finds

SIXTY-two per cent of voters want benefit cuts for migrants to help bring down the ballooning welfare bill, new polling shows.

Payment cuts to young people not in work was backed by just 38 per cent and 18 per cent would look for savings from those with mental health conditions.





Only thirty per cent support swinging reductions overall before pointing to where savings could be found, a poll carried out by Charlesbye and Merlin Strategy reveals. MUST

Labour attempted to bring down the welfare bill by £5 billion last summer but were thwarted by a rebellion by their backbench MPs.

The poll comes ahead of the local elections where Labour are expected to receive an electoral drubbing.

It also found that 14 per cent of those who defected would go back to Labour or the Tories.



A further 31 per cent would even look for another new party to back.

Overall, sixty-six per cent believe the country is heading on the wrong direction with only 21 per cent saying it’s going the right way.

Lee Cain, founding Partner at Charlesbye, said: “Voters have been demanding change for more than a decade, and Westminster’s traditional parties have shown themselves unable or unwilling to deliver it.

“The result is not a temporary flirtation with Reform or the Greens, but the permanent abandonment of the two main parties.



“If the insurgents disappoint, these voters will not come home – they will keep looking for something new.”

The findings were from a national poll of 4,209 adults from 2nd April 2026 to 16th April 2026.

News.title: Madeline McCann trolls should hang heads in shame – Like Kerry Needham, Kate and Gerry are in hell without extra agony
News.content:
IT has been 19 years since Madeleine McCann vanished during a family holiday on the Algarve.

Her 21-year-old sister Amelie — asleep in her cot at the time — probably doesn’t remember her, other than memories crafted through family recollections and photos.





But she and her twin Sean, now a strapping young man who towers over his sibling, attended a prayer vigil with their parents Gerry and Kate this week.

“The search goes on to find her, to achieve some justice, to make the world that bit safer,” they said in a joint statement.

Few could fail to sympathise with the McCann family.

Apart, that is, from those who still obsessively hector them online for leaving the kids alone in their holiday apartment while they dined with friends just a few metres away.

There can’t be a day goes by when they don’t think of their daughter, forever frozen in their minds at just three years old, and wonder where the hell she is.

Was she sold to someone else and has now all but forgotten where and who she came from? Or, following evidence highlighted in a bombshell Sun investigation, was she abducted by German paedophile Christian Brueckner and later killed?

He denies having anything to do with Madeleine’s disappearance, but police are keen to have him extradited here to potentially face trial. However, unless there’s hard evidence, the hope must always be there for her family that she might yet be found.

It’s the same hope that still flickers in the hearts of other parents whose children have gone missing.





Kerry Needham, whose toddler son Ben went missing in Greece in 1991, rejects the theory that he might be dead because there’s no physical or forensic evidence to prove it.

In fact, she’s currently waiting on the results of a DNA test from a man in the States who believes he might be her missing son. Truly torturous.

Another well-known case is 14-year-old Andrew Gosden, who left home in Doncaster in 2007, travelled to London and hasn’t been seen since.

His parents continue to live at the family home so he can find them, and his teenage bedroom remains as he left it.

The urgent desperation all these parents felt at the time their children went missing has gone, replaced by the day-to-day living hell of existing in a world that carries on as normal around you while you try to get through each hour still not knowing where they are.

It’s an unconscionable nightmare you wouldn’t wish on anyone.

So a memo to the McCann trolls: Be kinder. They’re already in hell without you piling on the agony.

CONTESTANTS for Celebrity Traitors have barely touched the tarmac at Inverness airport and already speculation has begun over who might win.

Names in the frame are the whip-smart ones including Miranda Hart, James Blunt, Amol Rajan, Michael Sheen and Professor Hannah Fry.

But as Prof Fry’s namesake Stephen proved last year, being regarded as highly intelligent draws suspicion. And the winner is nearly always the secretly wily person who everyone underestimates.



I’M THE TOOTH LAIRY

ROBBIE WILLIAMS is looking even more cheeky chappie than usual after his front tooth broke in half.

I lost a whole tooth just as I arrived at the Loose Women studios last week, and after a dash to Boots for some Poligrip, I avoided saying anything emphatic that might dislodge it and got through the show.

But a subsequent temporary solution has already fallen out and I’m currently awaiting some bridge contraption to tide me over until they can come up with something more permanent.

And all for the bargain price of 48 squillion pounds.

Needless to say, I won’t be sharing a photo of my predicament.

But let’s put it this way, if Stu Price from The Hangover put on a blonde wig, we’d be doppelgangers.

INMATES at HMP Usk in Monmouthshire can do yoga, crocheting classes, gym activities, take a walk in the sensory garden and hang out with therapy dogs.

I’ll have two weeks in July, please.

KILLER RIGHTS WRONG

AN in-depth report on the abuse suffered by ten-year-old Sara Sharif at the hands of her killer father Urfan is being kept secret by Surrey County Council.



It says it is doing so to protect his data protection rights.

Sara, who was sent to live with her father despite his 16-year history of attacking women and children, was let down by the authorities when she was alive.

And now she’s dead, they’re still letting her down.

In the name of truth, justice and the potential to learn valuable lessons, this report should be made public.

Who cares about a murderer’s supposed “rights”?

A WORD IN YOUR EAR, ZOE

MY youngest has reverted to wired headphones because, she reckons, they’re less likely to get nicked.

But it seems that global sales of the retro earpieces are up by 20 per cent for other reasons too, including the unreliability of Bluetooth.

Actress Zoe Kravitz, who may or may not be engaged to boyfriend Harry Styles, has lamented that a dodgy Bluetooth connection is “ruining important moments”.



She adds: “Imagine . . . you’re with someone on a date, you’re trying to set a vibe and then you have to forget the network. On a date!”

Er, right.

Cue all the baby boomers: “Why ruin an important moment by being on your phone in the first place?”

SO PRESSING INFLATABLE forceps have been used on 300 babies in the first “breakthrough innovation” for childbirth in decades. Experts say it offers a “gentle” experience with none of the bruising or injury associated with the old method. Invented by Argentinian mechanic Jorge Odon, it begs the question: Where the hell was he when I first gave birth 34 years ago? My eldest was a forceps birth and, following the use of the devil’s salad servers, she looked like she’d done four rounds with Mike Tyson, while I had to sit on a rubber ring for a month. Now, will someone please come up with an inflatable mammogram machine that negates the need to squish your breast tissue between two sheets of ice cold glass? All together now: “Sometimes it’s hard to be a woman . . . ”

READY TO PULL PLUG?

FORMER Made In Chelsea star Binky Felstead asked baker Reshmi Bennett to make a free cake for her son’s third birthday in exchange for her plugging the company on social media.

But Reshmi told her to stuff it, went public about the request, and then another bakery said they’d given her a free cake and she’d failed to plug it.

Now Binky has given an interview to say she has suffered “relentless abuse” online over the incident and pointed out that collaboration requests are “standard” in the world of influencers who peddle their perfectly curated, luxury lifestyle while sometimes flogging a product they’ve been well paid to promote.

Binky always puts “Ad” on such posts, while plenty don’t. But the world of “gifting” is a slightly greyer area.

One imagines that, along with the millions who follow the every move of their favourite influencer, there’s someone else keeping a very close eye on any “benefits in kind”.

HMRC.



ACADEMICS from Newcastle University have created an “artificial nose” that sniffs out when food in your fridge is about to go off.

What’s wrong with using your actual nose?

LIKELY STOREY

BUSINESSMAN Luke Perret has been ordered to demolish a £200,000 annexe built in his garden because it’s bigger than he was given permission for.

Mr Perret, 31, of Warrington, Cheshire, says his builder “used some artistic licence” to make changes and that they were both “naive” but claims, “we didn’t do this deliberately”.

So, despite having permission for a small, single-storey annexe with one bedroom, they accidentally built a much larger home with two beds, basement, study, walk-in wardrobe and two dormer windows?

A tall storey indeed.

News.title: I was so worried my local pub would close I remortgaged my house to buy it – I don’t even drink there that much
News.content:
A PENSIONER who could not bear to see his village pub close remortgaged his home to buy it — despite rarely drinking there himself.

Peter Manfield, 73, stepped in to save The Dog and Donkey in Knowle, near Budleigh Salterton, Devon, when it faced an uncertain future.





The pub, which dates back around 100 years and served locals through the Second World War, risked being sold off and potentially converted into flats.

Mr Manfield, a music teacher and musician, said he is “not a big drinker” and might visit “once a fortnight or once in 10 days” — often stopping in after work for a quiet pint.

Lacking the funds to buy it outright, he chose to remortgage his house to secure the £270,000 purchase in 2023 and carry out modest improvements.

He said: “It’s a lovely pub and the heart of the village. To lose it would have been catastrophic. Once that history is gone, you don’t get it back.”



Having lived in the village since 1997, he said the previous landlord had been struggling, raising fears the building could be redeveloped or even demolished.

Despite owning the premises, Mr Manfield insists he sees himself more as a custodian than a proprietor.



The pub retains original features including a fireplace, tiled floor and even a widened bar — installed during the war to stop American GIs leaping over it to flirt with barmaids.

Mr Manfield partnered with first-time landlord Mark Loftin, who took over the lease in February 2024.

The pair share a commitment to preserving the pub’s traditional character rather than turning it into a gastropub.



Community response has been overwhelmingly positive, with locals praising the effort to keep the venue alive.

Regulars include skittle teams, dog walkers and village groups.

His efforts come as new figures highlight the fragile state of Britain’s pub trade.

Around two pubs a day closed in the first three months of the year, according to the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA), with 161 shutting permanently — a 26% rise on the same period last year — and roughly 2,400 jobs lost.

The BBPA blamed rising labour costs, including increases to the minimum wage, alongside higher taxes.



Chief executive Emma McClarkin warned even profitable pubs were seeing earnings “wiped out by a disproportionate tax burden and huge costs”.

Scotland saw the highest number of closures, while the South East and London were also heavily affected.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Wales was the only part of the UK to record a net increase in pub numbers.

The government said it was supporting the sector through business rates relief, extended opening hours during the World Cup and a hospitality fund, but industry groups say more action is needed to stem the decline.

News.title: Costs & lack of govt action are killing pubs… it feels like a deliberate demolition of a treasured national institution
News.content:
PUBS are now closing at a rate of roughly two a day. Two a day.

Think about that. By the time you’ve finished your shift, had your dinner and put your feet up, another local will have shut its doors for good.





Lights off. Beer pumps dry. Community gone.

And this hasn’t just happened overnight.

This has been a slow, painful decline over the past 20 years, driven not by bad landlords or failing businesses, but by relentless pressure from the very people who are supposed to support British industry . . . government after government.

The great British pub isn’t just a place to have a pint. It’s part of who we are.



It’s where working people have always gone to unwind, to talk, to laugh, to forget about the stress of the day. It’s community, culture, and history.

And we’re watching it disappear.

Why?

Because the numbers simply don’t stack up any more.



Start with tax. Britain has some of the highest beer duty in the world.

It’s often pointed out that our beer tax is around ten times higher than Germany’s. Ten times.

And on top of that, pubs are effectively tax collectors, handing over 20 per cent VAT on what they sell. With VAT, duty and other levies, a £5.50 pint can include more than £2 in tax.

Meanwhile, across the continent, many countries have slashed VAT for hospitality to around ten per cent, to support the sector.

They understand its value, economically, culturally and socially.



Here? Nothing. Just more taxes, budget after budget.

Then you’ve got business rates. Sky-high, completely disproportionate and outdated. They cost me £45,000 a year.

A system that punishes bricks-and-mortar businesses while online giants laugh all the way to the bank.

Add rent to that. Again, disproportionately high for pubs. In many cases, completely unsustainable.

My backstreet pub, The Three Colts in Buckhurst Hill, Essex, pays £85,000 a year in rent and it’s no bigger than some of the houses nearby.



That’s the reality.

Landlords are paying through the nose just to keep the doors open. I show the football.

For that much-loved service for my regulars, Sky and TNT charge me £20,000 a year combined.

And then came the one-two punch that nearly finished most publicans off.

First, Covid. Restrictions that, for many pubs, felt completely detached from reality.



Doors shut. Trade gone overnight; any savings we had, wiped out. Loans taken out just to survive. Some simply never reopened.

Then straight into the energy crisis. And this wasn’t minor.

We’re talking £4,000 to £5,000 a month electricity bills for small pubs, mine included.



It was a lottery depending on when your contract renewed. Get it wrong, and that was it. Game over. Night night.

Many good landlords didn’t survive that. Many far better at the job than me.

And just when those who did thought they might be through the worst of it, along came the latest Budgets.

Rising National Insurance contributions. Increased wage pressures. More costs piled on.

The result? Jobs gone and shifts cut. In hospitality alone, around 150,000 jobs have disappeared in just two years.



Not because businesses don’t want staff, but because they simply can’t afford them. How is that helping anyone?

And here’s the reality politicians don’t seem to grasp at all.

You can’t just keep increasing wages and costs without consequences.

Of course people should earn more. Everyone agrees with that. But where does that money come from? It doesn’t just appear out of thin air.

It comes from somewhere, and right now it’s coming from reduced hours, fewer staff and, in many cases, that’s leading to closures.

At the same time, demand isn’t what it used to be. Since Covid, habits have changed.



People go out less. Younger generations are drinking less.

People have less disposable income, and in some areas the demographics have changed so much that the majority won’t drink for religious reasons.

So pubs are now caught in a perfect storm: Fewer customers, but with higher costs.

That is a business model heading in one direction.

And it’s not because landlords aren’t good enough. I know landlords far better than me who have lost everything.



Good people, running good pubs, doing everything right . . . wiped out through no fault of their own.

So what needs to change?

How do we save the great British pub?

First, VAT. A cut from 20 per cent to something closer to ten would be a game changer.

It would ease pressure, improve cash flow and help bring prices down for customers.



Second, proper business rates reform.

Pubs should not be rated on turnover alone, as this does not take into account the increasingly high costs of running a pub, such as energy and wages.

The 15 per cent temporary cut is an insult.

That needs to be multiplied several times — an emergency 75 per cent relief, as happened during Covid, for something like six months would allow pubs to reset.

Third, incentivise us to take on new staff. Employers’ National Insurance contributions must be reversed.



Right now, it feels like pubs are being punished, not supported.

At times, it even feels like a deliberate demolition of one of this country’s most treasured pastimes.

And here’s the bigger point:

If we lose the great British pub, we lose something far bigger than a place to drink.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

We lose community. We lose heritage. We lose culture.



We lose one of the very things that makes this country what it is.

News.title: Inside secret American city where all residents live together in Cold War tower block & most only leave ‘in a hearse’
News.content:
AS barmaid Beverly Sue Walts sits down for a well-earned break, she leans over and tells me: “Welcome to America’s most secret town. We call it the town under one roof.”

I have made one of the strangest journeys of my life to a remote outpost in Alaska, tucked between mountains and the sea.



But if you are imagining a picturesque huddle of houses clinging to the ends of the Earth, think again.

Instead, here stands an imposing 14-storey Cold War block called Begich Towers — or simply “BTI” — where all 200 of the city of Whittier’s residents live self-sufficiently.

A former army barracks, the building is a mini universe, complete with post office, grocery store, a hotel and a church — and it can only be accessed via an underground World War Two tunnel. There’s even a communal pet reindeer called Manu.



Hotel owner June Miller, 79, from Minnesota, who has lived here for 35 years, says: “This building is the town. If you don’t want to leave, you don’t have to.

“We are visited by dentists and doctors, and there are hairdressers and dog groomers.

“Rumour has it that some folks have not stepped out for weeks, months and even years. It’s the most unique town in the world.”

Finding my way to this place, just under 60 miles from the city of Anchorage, wasn’t easy.

‘Out of a Bond movie’

You can only get to Whittier by sea (cruise ships stop there) or via a two-mile rail tunnel carved through the mountains. It was converted in 2000 to allow vehicles through but as they share a single lane with the trains, it only runs one way at any given time. And it closes every night at 10.30pm



Then there’s the weather.

The 60mph winter winds are brutal, 30ft of snowfall is common and it rains six months a year, earning it the title of the wettest inhabited place in the whole of the US.

That’s why residents have everything they need under one roof.

Veteran Gary Gibson, 80, explains: “The BTI was designed by the US military and built in 1957 when it was used as barracks for the soldiers and their families.

“It then transitioned for residential use when they left in the 1960s. It was convenient to keep it that way because of the harsh weather.



“There are also tunnels all through Whi­tt­­ier leading to the BTI — it is straight out of a James Bond movie.”

Such is Whittier’s seclusion that the US military stationed a secret war base there in the 1940s.

Entering the BTI, I was hit by an oppressive smell of old cigarette smoke mixed with cleaning fluids. The halls are stark and prison-like — but no one judges you.



Often ­people run errands in their pyjamas, walking between floors in their socks and slippers.

Gary, who moved to the town six years ago, and sips Cherry Coke from a flask he brings to the local bar every evening, adds: “So many people know nothing about this town. It was designed to be hidden and it has stayed hidden.

“Most of the people are hiding here from the law or running from ­something.”

That’s true of Lorena Galvban, 37, who is the town’s janitor, and tells me she moved into the building last ­September from Argentina after escaping an abusive relationship.

She reveals: “I came here with my two children to hide for a couple of months after an 11-year abusive relationship.



“But we haven’t left as the children are so happy. They can run about and be free.

“I work here, live here and spend my life here.”

She lives on the first floor and her kids, aged nine and ten, watch TV on their iPads in the hallway, which is used as a communal living room.



As I walk those very same halls, I am struck by how much the building feels like a working town — only here the rush-hour commute means a stop on every floor on the elevator.

The town is watched over by gener­al manager Dan Johnson who says with a laugh: “Of course people leave — in a hearse.”

Dan, who has lived here for decades, ensures the building ticks. He fixes the lifts, which break ­regularly, and carries out general maintenance.

On the first floor I find the post office, shop Kozy Korner which imports food from Anchorage, and the launderette, all run by residents, as well as the notary public’s office.

The basement houses the church and each morning 50 of the town’s kids take the 30-second journey down to floor B to go through the tunnel which leads to their school.



Although forbidden, some spend their lunchtime hanging out in the lobby, which seems to act as an extension of the school’s playground.

The pupils’ ages range from five to 16 and most of teachers also live in the building.

As some of the flats are tiny, there are big industrial-style freezers where locals can store extra food and a maze of storage cases.

On the second floor, there’s a gym and a library. It is also home to a mayor, firemen and paramedics.



There used to be a jail inside the towers but a police station was recently built and is connected via one of the building’s many tunnels.

‘Hook-ups are common’

Mayor Victor Shen, 37, who was born in the BTI, lives here with his wife Bibo, 43, and three young children.

He says: “The only thing that’s changed here is the paint. It’s home, it’s unique and my family is here. My mum lives upstairs and I’ve been here since I was a baby. I was here when you could only get out via a train through the tunnel and it was expensive, so people rarely left.

“The fact it’s harder to leave the town makes it more of a community.”

There is only one way to blow off steam — at the all-year-round makeshift bar, featuring two pool tables and a broken Pac-Man arcade game.



It is frequented by a woman named only as “The Boss” who wears sunglasses and manically rips open one dollar scratchcards one after the other, shouting: “I love gambling.”

Beverly, a 64-year-old blonde bombshell, doesn’t bat an eyelid, and reveals: “I’ve worked at the bar for 35 years and lived in the BTI in the same apartment for 34 years.

“I moved here from Texas with my then-husband and I was going to work here one summer but I met another guy and I didn’t leave.”

She tells me that because there is no one else in town, people usually meet at the bar and hook-ups between residents are common.

Beverly said: “This is like the town’s dating site — that or the hallways. If you like the look of someone usually you can get them because there’s not many people to choose from.”



But Beverly admits: “It is so isolated it can be a bit of a deathtrap.

“My 35-year-old son died from heart failure because an ambulance wasn’t able to come in time. But I still love this place.”

Frank Doty, 42, who is dating fellow resident and OnlyFans model Jaycee Katchatag, 22, agrees: “We love it. It’s a small community and everyone knows everyone.

“You don’t have to leave the block to do anything and we prefer it like that — everything is there at the push of an elevator button.

“Life is here so why would we want to leave?” Not everyone is a fan of the towers.



Kris Adams, 31, who is staying at the BTI while working on the railroads, says: “The place is a hellhole.

“There’s a constant smell of fryer grease and there are cockroaches. But they say the higher up you get the less bugs you have.”

I certainly didn’t spot any cockroaches while staying in one of June’s two-bedroom 15th floor apartments which she rents out to holidaymakers.

‘Soviet horror movie’

The flat — which has a spectacular view — feels like you are stepping into an elderly relative’s home with its 1980s furnishings and boxes of tissues dotted around.

At her apartment next door, June tells me: “I moved here in 1990 from Minnesota and never looked back.”



Of the BTI, she continued: “We don’t have much land here, we are a piece of pie surrounded by mountains, glaciers and water, so they had to build up.

“There’s barely anything else but this building.

“But we lead a life of Riley because you don’t have to start the car to go and check your boat — you just go down the elevator, go through a couple of the secret tunnels, and you’re there within five minutes.

“Your friends are your neighbours so you can pop down in pyjamas.”

But, whipping out binoculars, she disagrees things can stay hidden in the town, saying with a wink: “I use these to see the comings and goings outside. I see which husbands are misbehaving.”



She shows me the church, where she goes to pray for sick residents. It can be accessed only with a code.

“We built this so we have a place of prayer and there’s a service every Sunday,” she says.

I am told there is little crime here, bar some drunken fights, as people prefer to sort things out themselves.

The towers are also scattered with dozens of cameras, making theft hard.

One call to the people manning the tunnel and you are unable to leave.



As it is time for me to leave the town, war hero Gary (who confesses he has a crush on Beverly) whispers to me: “I’ve served three tours in Vietnam and Panama.

“I’ve been shot at and been in three helicopters that have been shot down.

“I’ve been all over the world. But I’ve never been anywhere like this. It might look like a Soviet horror movie but it sucks you in.”

And I can’t help but silently agree as I ponder packing it all in and moving to Whittier, where I can spend my nights crooning with Beverly.

News.title: Zack Polanski’s refusal to root out the Gaza-obsessed racists in Green party is now disturbing and putting off voters
News.content:
Call out hate

ZACK Polanski likes to make attractive fantasy promises about protecting people from “rip-off Britain”, saving the planet through Net Zero and spending an extra £30billion on the NHS.

But in recent days the mask has well and truly slipped.





His shocking suggestion that Jews may only be feeling a “perception” of antisemitism rather than their hideous daily experience of the real thing — alongside his attack on brave cops who disarmed a Jew-hunting knifeman in Golders Green — have revealed the sinister face of Green Party “populism”.

Polanski describes himself as proudly Jewish.

But his refusal to root out the Gaza-obsessed racists in his own ranks is now filtering through to ordinary voters who have become increasingly disturbed and put off.

Polanski’s plummeting approval ratings are no cause for any kind of complacency from the Government.

Even as Keir Starmer launched a talking shop yesterday to tackle antisemitism, counter-terror cops were launching a probe into another arson attack on a former Jewish synagogue.

Beyond demanding the Arts Council claw back taxpayer money spent by woke charities on promoting anti-Israel bile, what did Starmer really hope to achieve beyond the usual verbal condemnation?

It might help if ministers had the courage to actually call out the hateful Islamist ideology responsible for Jews living in daily fear.

Tax attacks

WHEN will Labour realise that taxing everything in sight isn’t the answer to fixing the nation’s finances?



The Mansion Tax hasn’t even come into force yet and is already set to cost the Treasury £400million.

Meanwhile, plans for pay-per-mile road tax on new electric cars will slash sales at a time when the Government wants drivers to make the switch.

Relentless taxation doesn’t grow the economy. It kills it stone dead.

A bad bet

IN a strong intervention, the Labour MP whose seat includes Doncaster Racecourse warns of the potential danger posed by affordability checks on punters.

Sally Jameson said an “intrusive or unreliable regime” would not only risk driving people to the illegal black market, depriving the Treasury of tax revenue.



It would also imperil jobs and threaten the viability of racing itself.

The PM’s wife, Lady Victoria, is a keen supporter of Doncaster races and the St Leger which this year celebrates its 250th anniversary.

Ministers must halt the checks or risk a historic mistake.

News.title: Serial paedo, 33, jailed for life over string of child sex offences as cops praise brave girl for helping to catch fiend
News.content:
LOCKED UP Serial paedo, 33, jailed for life over string of child sex offences as cops praise brave girl for helping to catch fiend

A MAN has been sentenced to life behind bars after pleading guilty to nine child sex offences.

Cops have praised the “bravery” of his victim after the girl’s heartbreaking statement was read out in court against the serial paedophile.



Sean McDade, 33 from Northampton, abused the child between May and July last year.



He was already a registered sex offender at the time.

The victim’s statement was read to the court last week (April 30) where she explained that he forced her not to tell anyone about his twisted actions.

The statement read: “He scared me and made me think I would get in trouble if I told anyone.”

However, the child did tell someone, which led to an investigation into McDade and his subsequent arrest.

McDade was charged with six counts of assault by penetration of a girl under 13, three counts of raping a girl under 13, and one count of causing/inciting a child under 13 to engage in sexual activity.

He pled guilty at Northampton Crown Court and was sentenced to life in prison with a minimum term of 12 years.

Lead investigator, Detective Constable Kirstie Brooks from Northamptonshire Police’s Child Abuse Investigation Unit, said: “I would like to commend the child in this case for their bravery, and I hope the conclusion of this case allows them to move forward onto brighter things.

“Although no sentence can ever take away what happened, I hope it brings them comfort that their abuser will now go to prison for a long time, and hopefully they can move on and finally get the life they deserve.



“Sean McDade is now where he belongs and we will continue working hard to put more people like him behind bars.”

Detective Superintendent Jen Castle said: “This was an immensely challenging case involving an extremely manipulative and depraved offender however despite the complexity, DC Brooks approached every stage with professionalism, resilience and compassion.

“As a direct result of her work, the child in this case did not have to give evidence and I am grateful to her for the skill and sensitivity she demonstrated throughout the investigation.”

News.title: KEIR STARMER: 'On Thursday you have a choice - here's where we'd be if Reform, Tories or Greens were in power'
News.content:
KEIR STARMER: 'On Thursday you have a choice - here's where we'd be if Reform, Tories or Greens were in power'

Prime Minister Keir Starmer urges voters to choose 'progress' over 'the politics of anger' as millions prepare to cast their ballots in a make-or-break set of local elections

View Image Keir Starmer said his rivals had shown themselves 'unfit for high office' (Image: PA)

Politics is about choices. The choices that affect you and your family.

‌



On Thursday, when you go to put your vote in the ballot box, there’s a clear choice on that piece of paper. Unity or division. Progress versus the politics of anger. The right plan for our country up against easy answers that will lead us nowhere.

‌



A Labour council working with our Labour Government to deliver your local services, or Reform who are intent on driving a wedge between our communities.

‌



Our country has faced huge challenges in recent decades. Together the British people have stood firm in the face of Tory austerity, the challenges Brexit has brought, the pandemic and the Conservatives recklessly trashing our economy with Liz Truss.

We’ve got through these tough times by standing together in the hope of a better future. Not by dividing our great nation. It’s that better future that my Labour Government is working every day to deliver alongside you.

Tearful veteran gives chilling Iran war warning about Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch READ MORE :

And today, as you know, we face even more challenges. I’ve been clear from the start that the war in Iran is not our war – but we know there’s a cost to that conflict that is being felt across Britain right now. And it’s a cost that will likely get worse in the coming months.

‌



What such global instability demands is strong leadership. That’s why I’ve never wavered in saying that we will not be dragged into this conflict. It simply wouldn’t have been in Britain’s national interest to do so.

Nigel Farage and Tory Leader Kemi Badenoch would have seen our Armed Forces deployed headfirst into a war with no plan and not so much as a second thought for the consequences here at home.

If they had been in power, their reckless actions would have put lives on the line abroad and hammered family finances here at home. They have both proven that they are unfit for high office.

‌



Meanwhile Green Party Leader Zack Polanski still believes that the UK should leave NATO and turn our backs on our international allies – just when global cooperation has scarcely been more important.

If that weren’t bad enough, he shamefully questioned the actions of the brave police officers who ran towards danger to apprehend the alleged suspect of the appalling antisemitic terror attack in Golders Green. He is completely unfit to lead the Green Party.

Farage, Badenoch and Polanski have proven they cannot meet this moment. But my Labour Government is.

‌



As your Prime Minister, I stand by the promise of change I made you nearly 2 years ago outside Downing Street. We must continue that important work and deliver a renewed Britain for you and your family. There’s much more to do, but together we’re making real progress.

We said we’d make work pay – and we have. With a pay boost for over 2 million low paid workers and the biggest boost to workers’ rights in a generation.

We said we’d give the next generation the best start in life – and we are. By lifting half a million kids out of poverty after we scrapped the Tories’ cruel 2 child limit.

Article continues below

We said we’d fix our NHS – and we are. Waiting lists are down by over 400,000 and we’ve hired 2,000 new GPs.

While others talk, Labour is delivering for you. Back action to ease the cost of living. Back our NHS. Back a better future for your local community. On Thursday, choose unity over division. Vote Labour.

News.title: Keir Starmer urges Brits 'choose progress over politics of anger' and details what Labour's delivered so far
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Keir Starmer urges Brits 'choose progress over politics of anger' and details what Labour's delivered so far

Keir Starmer said Labour’s rivals had proven they cannot meet the moment after Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage rushed to back Donald Trump’s war in the Middle East

View 3 Images Keir Starmer issued a rallying cry to voters ahead the crunch local elections (Image: Getty Images)

Keir Starmer has urged voters to choose “unity over division” in a rallying cry ahead of a high-stakes set of local elections.

‌



The Prime Minister said the country must face the huge challenges left by austerity, the Covid pandemic, Brexit and Liz Truss's calamitous mini Budget - coupled with the impact of the war in Iran - by standing together. Writing in the Mirror, he appealed to to the public to choose progress towards a better future over the "politics of anger" at the ballot box on Thursday.

‌



Mr Starmer said Labour’s rivals had proven they cannot meet this moment, after Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage rushed to back Donald Trump’s war in the Middle East. And he lashed out at Green Party leader Zack Polanski for pushing to quit Nato and sharing a social media post criticising the police response to the antisemitic terror attack in Golders Green.

‌



View 3 Images The PM urged voters to reject Nigel Farage's Reform (Image: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

It comes as millions of people prepare to head to the polls on Thursday across England, Wales and Scotland in the Labour Government's biggest electoral test since its landslide win in 2024.

‌



Pollsters have delivered doom-laden predictions that Labour could shed hundreds of councillors in England, lose control in Wales and fall well short of victory in Scotland, in a nightmare set of results less than two years on from the general election.

But Mr Starmer has come out fighting as he promised voters there was more to do to fix the mess left behind by the Tories.

In an article for the Mirror, the Prime Minister said: “Politics is about choices. The choices that affect you and your family. On Thursday, when you go to put your vote in the ballot box, there’s a clear choice on that piece of paper.

‌



"Unity or division. Progress versus the politics of anger. The right plan for our country up against easy answers that will lead us nowhere.”

View 3 Images The PM issued a rallying cry ahead of the local elections (Image: Lauren Hurley / No 10 Downing Street)

He added: "Farage, Badenoch and Polanski have proven they cannot meet this moment. But my Labour Government is."

‌



The fallout from the elections could be make-or-break for the Prime Minister as speculation swirls over whether he could face a leadership challenge.

Angela Rayner and Wes Streeting are tipped as contenders for the keys to No10 but neither appear keen to wield the knife. Andy Burnham has made little secret of his leadership ambitions but he is not an MP - barring him from standing in a leadership contest.

The PM's allies are ramping up efforts to see off a plot if Labour tensions erupt in the aftermath of the local elections.

‌



Communities Secretary Steve Reed, a staunch ally of the PM, urged MPs against Tory-style "doom-scrolling" through leaders if Labour suffers a hammering at the polls. Many MPs are “sick and tired of all this psychodrama”, he said.

He added: "The whole notion that we would copy the Conservatives and go doom-scrolling through leaders in a way that means the government is completely incapable of dealing with the things that matter the most to the British public is an absolute nonsense. And I'm not going to engage in it, and most of our MPs would not engage in it either."

Article continues below

A group of angry backbenchers is said to be plotting to break ranks and call for his resignation in an open letter in the aftermath. But Tom Watson, who was involved in a similar plot to oust Tony Blair, warned it was a mistake that risked damaging Labour and handing ammunition to its opponents.

He wrote on his Substack: "If Labour has lost support to Reform, the Greens, the Liberal Democrats and the Conservatives, the solution cannot simply be a different name on the door. The party has to listen harder, think deeper and recover its political purpose.

"So, with the greatest respect to any colleague tempted by this course: that was then and this is now. Do not do it. Really, do not. If I had my time again, I would not have signed the letter in 2006."

News.title: Donald Trump reignites feud with the Pope with 'unacceptable' remarks
News.content:
Donald Trump reignites feud with the Pope with 'unacceptable' remarks

It comes as Secretary of State Marco Rubio prepared to make a diplomatic visit to the Vatican in a bid to mend relations with the Holy See

View Image (Image: AP)

Donald Trump has reignited his feud with Pope Leo XIV with "unacceptable" remarks about nuclear weapons.

‌



It comes as Secretary of State Marco Rubio prepared to make a diplomatic visit to the Vatican in a bid to mend relations with the Holy See.

‌



Trump again accused Leo in an interview Tuesday of being “OK for Iran to have a nuclear weapon.” Leo has said no such thing and Catholic Church teaching says the mere possession of nuclear weapons is “immoral.”

‌



And he claimed the Pope's rhetoric was "endangering a lot of Catholics, and a lot of people".

Speaking to reporters Tuesday, Pope Leo hit back at the claims, saying the Catholic Church “for years has spoken out against all nuclear weapons, so there is no doubt there.”

Leo doubled down on his insistence that his call for peace and dialogue in the U.S-Israeli war in Iran is Biblically inspired.

‌



“I’ve spoken from the first moment of being elected, and we’re near the anniversary: I said ‘Peace be with you,’” Leo said as he left his country house in Castel Gandolfo.

“The mission of the church is to preach the Gospel, to preach peace. If someone wants to criticize me for announcing the Gospel, let him do it with the truth,” Leo said. “And so I hope simply to be listened to about the value of the Word of God.”

Italy defended the Pope and his call for peace and dialogue in the Iran war.

‌



Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said in a social media post Thursday that Trump’s attacks “are neither acceptable nor helpful to the cause of peace.”

In an interview with conservative commentator Hugh Hewitt, Trump claimed the pontiff is helping Iran and making the world less safe with his comments about the importance of not treating immigrants with disrespect.

“The Pope would rather talk about the fact that it’s OK for Iran to have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said in the interview on Monday. “And I don’t think that’s very good. I think he’s endangering a lot of Catholics and a lot of people. I guess if it's up to the Pope, he thinks it's just fine for Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

‌



The Pope has not said Iran should obtain nuclear weapons. He’s called for more peace talks, and criticised war with Iran generally and Trump’s specific threats of mass civilian strikes. The pope also has emphasised that he’s reflecting biblical and church teachings, not speaking as a political rival to Trump.

Regardless, Trump’s latest comments may make Rubio’s task more difficult when he sees the pontiff on Thursday. Rubio has often been called on to tone down or explain Trump’s harsh rhetoric as it relates to Europe, NATO and the Middle East, but the president’s dispute with the pope has domestic political implications in the U.S. with midterm congressional elections approaching.

Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani added: “I reaffirm my support for every action and word of Pope Leo; his words are a testament to dialogue, the value of human life, and freedom. This is a vision shared by our government, which is committed through diplomacy to ensuring stability and peace in all areas where conflicts exist."

‌



Rubio is due to meet with Leo on Thursday and is due to see Tajani and Premier Giorgia Meloni on Friday.

The State Department said on Monday that Rubio, a practicing Catholic who after this trip will have visited Italy or the Vatican at least three times in the past year, would travel to Rome and Vatican City on Thursday and Friday.

Trump lashed out at Leo on social media last month, saying the pope was soft on crime and terrorism for comments about the administration’s immigration policies and deportations as well as the Iran war. Leo then said God doesn’t listen to the prayers of those who wage war.

Article continues below

Later, Trump posted a social media image likening himself to Jesus Christ, which he then deleted after backlash. He has refused to apologize to Leo and has sought to explain away the social media post by saying he thought the image was of him as a doctor.

The tension has spilled over into Italian politics, with Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, a long-time Trump ally whom Rubio is also expected to meet this week, taking exception to Trump’s comments about the pope.

Trump in return criticised her as his ire against NATO allies expands over what he sees as a lack of support for the Iran war — most recently with the Pentagon planning to pull thousands of troops out of Germany in the coming months.

News.title: Inside Blake Lively and Justin Baldoni settlement – and who really won
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Inside Blake Lively and Justin Baldoni settlement – and who really won

According to a PR expert, Blake Lively and Justin Baldoni's settlement is less a win and more damage control to avoid further fallout as the actress makes a very public statement at the Met Gala

View 4 Images Blake Lively and Justin Baldoni have been at loggerheads since the release of It Ends With Us (Image: AP)

After months of speculation and mounting public scrutiny, the dispute between Blake Lively and Justin Baldoni has finally drawn to a close with a carefully worded joint statement. But while the legal battle may be over, the question remains: who actually came out on top?

‌



According to PR expert Mayah Riaz, the answer is far from straightforward. "I'd say that from a PR perspective, this settlement feels like it's less like a victory lap and more like a mutual surrender," she explains. "Neither Blake nor Justin comes out of this completely unscathed, but both have clearly realised that dragging this through a very public trial would have caused even deeper reputational damage."

‌



The joint statement itself is telling. Heavy on phrases like "moving forward", "respectful workplaces" and "closure", it avoids any admission of fault while signalling a shared desire to bring the saga to an end.

‌



Heidi Klum's Met Gala outfit takes bold theme to a whole new level READ MORE :

Blake Lively goes solo to Met Gala as Justin Baldoni lawsuit ends in joint statement READ MORE :

View 4 Images Blake Lively appeared hours after the settlement was announced at the Met Gala (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

In a rare move, the pair issued a joint statement via their lawyers, saying: "Raising awareness, and making a meaningful impact in the lives of domestic violence survivors - and all survivors - is a goal that we stand behind.

"It is our sincere hope that this brings closure and allows all involved to move forward constructively and in peace, including a respectful environment online."

‌



The terms of the settlement were not disclosed. Mayah adds: "The wording is incredibly polished and carefully crafted to avoid liability. This is usually PR code for 'everyone involved wants this story to finally stop dominating headlines.'"

So who "won"? In reality, Mayah suggest the only clear victory is damage limitation. Blake arguably regained a degree of control by shifting the narrative back towards her career and public persona - a pivot that was on full display just hours after the settlement at the Met Gala

"Her appearance was very telling and felt like a relaunch," Mayah says. "Attending so soon after the settlement looked strategic. It sent a visual message of resilience and composure - but it also felt like she was dressing herself out of a crisis."

‌



View 4 Images Ryan Reynolds was also dragged into the scandal with his wife and co-star Justin Baldoni (Image: TheStewartofNY, WireImagevia Getty Images)

While Baldoni avoided a prolonged and highly public trial, one that risked keeping allegations tied to his name for years, both sides sidestepped potentially greater fallout.

However the longer-term impact may be harder to shake - particularly for Blake and her husband, Ryan Reynolds.

‌



"I do think this saga has dented Blake and Ryan Reynolds' untouchable Hollywood power-couple image," Mayah explains. "Before this, they were widely seen as universally liked, witty and media-savvy. Now, public opinion is far more divided and once that perception cracks, it's difficult to fully repair."

That shift was subtly reflected at the Met Gala itself. While the actress has historically dominated the event, this year felt different.

"In previous years, Blake and Ryan often felt like the unofficial royalty of the Met Gala," Mayah notes. "This time, the spotlight seemed more cautious around them. That's the difference between being famous and being untouchable."

‌



View 4 Images Justin Baldoni issued a counter lawsuit (Image: WireImage)

Still, there were signs of a deliberate image reset. Blake leaned into softer, more personal styling choices, including subtle references to her children - a move Mayah sees as calculated.

"That kind of imagery helps reposition her away from controversy and back towards relatability and warmth," she says.

Article continues below

"Both parties reached the point where continuing the battle risked overshadowing their careers," Mayah concludes. "In Hollywood, sometimes settling quietly is the closest thing anyone gets to winning."

News.title: Princess Eugenie's pregnancy announcement sends 'clear message' from King Charles
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Princess Eugenie's pregnancy announcement sends 'clear message' from King Charles

Buckingham Palace announced Princess Eugenie's pregnancy on Monday, with one royal insider claiming it shows their loyalty to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's daughter despite the ongoing fallout from his latest scandal

View 3 Images Buckingham Palace announced the news on Monday

Princess Eugenie's pregnancy announcement may have seemed like a straightforward piece of happy royal news, but according to one expert, the way it was delivered speaks volumes about her standing within the Firm.

The announcement was shared via Buckingham Palace, rather than through a more personal or private channel - a detail that royal commentator Afua Acheampong-Hagan believes is highly significant.

"I think it is interesting that, although there was a post on social media as well, that the official announcement came from Buckingham Palace," she explains. "I think this does mean she is clearly still in favour with the royal family."

Princess Eugenie reveals she is pregnant with baby three in sweet social media return READ MORE :

View 3 Images Fergie has remained out of the spotlight since the latest Epstein files revealed email exchanges between her and the sex offender (Image: Getty Images)

Far from being a routine update, Afua suggests the move signals something more deliberate and protective.

"I think it also gives her a bit of protection at this time," she says. "A delicate time, early pregnancy, but also that kind of umbrella gathering in of the royal family announcing signifies, 'She's still under our wing, she's under our protection, she's taken care of'."

In other words, the Palace stepping in to make the announcement sends a subtle but firm message internally and publicly about Eugenie's place within the monarchy amid a wave of scandal surrounding her parents Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and Sarah Ferguson.

"It's kind of a bit of a 'Back off, we're protecting this girl, our granddaughter, our niece, at this delicate time, and that's why we're announcing'," Afua adds.

The wording of the statement itself also raised eyebrows, particularly its closing line referencing King Charles III. "I also think it's significant that they wrote at the end that the King is delighted," Afua notes. "Again, it's that reiteration that she's been protected - that she's beloved by the royal family, that she's been taken under the wing of the King."

View 3 Images Eugenie shared sweet snaps of her baby scan (Image: Princess Eugenie/Buckingham Palace)

For royal watchers, these carefully chosen details point to a coordinated effort to reinforce Eugenie's position within the family and to project unity at a time when the monarchy remains under intense public scrutiny. "I think all these things are quite significant," Afua concludes. "It was deliberately done in that way."

Andrew and Fergie have kept under the radar since the latest Epstein files revealed email exchanges between the pair and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Its thought Andrew is hiding away on the Sandringham Estate after being forced out of his Royal Lodge home in Windsor, while Fergie is said to be "couch surfing" following the eviction.

Article continues below

Buckingham Palace announced Eugenie's pregnancy on Saturday, alongside a statement reading: " Her Royal Highness Princess Eugenie and Mr Jack Brooksbank are very pleased to announce that they are expecting their third child together, due this summer.

"August (aged five) and Ernest (aged two) are also very excited to have another sibling join the family. His Majesty The King has been informed and is delighted with the news."

News.title: Stepmother is accused of killing girl, 5, in scalding hot bath
News.content:
Stepmother is accused of killing girl, 5, in scalding hot bath

Janice Nix, 66, denied killing her stepdaughter Andrea Bernard who died after she suffered 50 per cent burns to her body when she was allegedly forced into the hot bath

View 3 Images Janice Nix has denied manslaughter (Image: PA)

A stepmother accused of killing a five-year-old girl with a scalding hot bath allegedly told the child's young brother that she would not hit him again if he claimed it was an accident, a court has heard.

Janice Nix, 67, has denied manslaughter against Andrea Bernard by punishing her with a hot bath in Thornton Heath, south London, on June 6 1978.

The defendant, of Clapham, south London, has also denied cruelty to Andrea's brother Desmond Bernard between October 1 1975 and June 6 1978, when he was seven to nine years old.

Andrea's death was treated as an accident for nearly half a century until her brother contacted police with new information in September 2022, Isleworth Crown Court heard at the trial opening on Tuesday.

During voluntary police interview, Nix gave a "completely different" version of events to the one she provided the coroner in 1978, prosecutor Kerry Broome said. Mr Bernard had approached the force after his sister's death "had become a burden he could no longer carry", she added.

View 3 Images Nix, pictured previously outside Uxbridge Magistrates' Court, denied the charges against her (Image: PA)

The defendant had been in a relationship with the children's father, also named Desmond Bernard, and was in effect their stepmother, the court heard.

Nix, then called Janice Thomas and in her late teenage years, had the main responsibility for their care as their father was often away working as a chauffeur, jurors were told.

Mr Bernard told police that Andrea "had been blamed for something" on the evening before the bath, but he could not recall what. Consequently, Nix said the girl could not go to school and must stay behind and clean, he claimed.

"Desmond knew this meant Andrea would be beaten, but recalls being relieved it would not be him", Ms Broome summarised. The boy discovered his sister was at school and assumed she "was no longer in trouble", the court heard.

"Given what happened later, it may have been... that Andrea had escaped the house and went to school without the defendant's knowledge, which made her very angry indeed", the prosecutor said.

View 3 Images The allegations were brought forward by Andrea's brother in 2022 (Image: PA)

Nix was "fuming" when they returned home together - hitting Andrea and shouting that she had told her to remain at home, Mr Bernard told police.

He claimed he went straight to his bedroom and could hear Nix beating Andrea through his bedroom door. He said he then heard her walk into the bathroom next door and water starting to run, around 15 to 30 minutes after the children had arrived.

He allegedly heard Nix call for Andrea to get in the bath, and Ms Broome told jurors: "Desmond could not see what was happening in the bathroom, but he heard Andrea screaming, and saying `it's hot, it's hot.

"Janice kept shouting at her to get in. He says `Andrea would not stop screaming and I can't remember how long it went on for, but then it just stopped'."

Nix told his sister to wake up before asking him to come into the room, Mr Bernard told police. He claimed she was cradling a "limp" Andrea in a towel and she was not awake.

The prosecution summarised: "Janice seemed scared and asked him to say it was an accident and that Andrea fell into the bath. She promised never to hit him again if he said that, so that is what he did: he told everyone it was an accident, and Janice never hit him again."

During the inquest, Nix had claimed that Andrea and her brother had looked dirty when they returned from school at about 4pm.

She said she told the children to have a bath upstairs, put on clean clothes and come back to the garden - the boy went first, the court heard.

Andrea was upstairs for about 15 to 20 minutes which "did not really seem a long time to me, she is a bit slow", Nix said. The girl returned to the garden wearing a dress and complaining of itchy legs, the defendant had claimed.

‌



She added that she "did not hear her call out at all" and it would have been possible to pick that up. Andrea's skin on her leg was reddish and peeling off as she scratched it, she said.

Nix also told the inquest that Andrea had fainted and an ambulance took her to the Mayday Hospital, Croydon, south London. "She did not say anything on the way to hospital about what had happened to her", she told the coroner.

Decades later, Nix told police that she had immediately run to the bathroom after hearing Andrea screaming. The girl was scrambling to get out of the bath and Nix lifted her out, she said.

‌



Her neighbour James Henry followed Nix into the house and gave her something to wrap Andrea in, she said. The child had "water blisters" on her skin and Mr Henry drove her to Mayday Hospital, she said.

The defendant also claimed that Mr Bernard made false allegations against her because he felt short-changed by his father's inheritance.

In addition, she told officers: "Andrea died as a result of a tragic accident caused by a malfunctioning boiler which overheated the water used for the bath."

Article continues below

It is not disputed that Andrea died in hospital on July 13 1978 as a result of complications from the burn injuries. Silver-haired Nix appeared in court wearing a blue jacket and trousers, a beige blouse, and glasses. For a large portion of proceedings she stared directly at Ms Broome who was speaking.

The trial continues.

News.title: Teacher accused of abusing and murdering baby 'said 'I f***ing killed him' in A&E'
News.content:
Teacher accused of abusing and murdering baby 'said 'I f***ing killed him' in A&E'

Jamie Varley, 37, who is accused of murdering and sexually abusing 13-month-old Preston Davey, allegedly told a doctor 'I f***ing killed him', Preston Crown Court has heard

View 4 Images

A teacher accused of murdering a baby allegedly said "I f***ing killed him" as a doctor attempted to resuscitate the child in a hospital A&E department, a court has heard.

‌



Jamie Varley, 37, is accused of killing and sexually abusing 13-month-old Preston Davey, who he was in the process of his adopting with his 32-year-old partner John McGowan-Fazackerley. Preston died at Blackpool Victoria Hospital in July 2023 after suffering 40 injuries over a four-month period while in the couple's care, prosecutors allege.

‌



The two men, of Grimsargh, Preston, are on trial at Preston Crown Court charged with a string of offences against the baby. McGowan-Fazackerley is alleged to have allowed the child's death. Both deny all charges.

‌



On Tuesday, the jury heard evidence on day six of the trial. Jurors were told medics worked on Preston for around an hour after he was brought into the hospital in cardiac and respiratory arrest.

View 4 Images Jamie Varley, 37, is accused of killing baby Preston (Image: X)

Dr Wendy Aubrey, the anaesthetist tasked with intubating Preston, told the court she responded to an emergency call in A&E and arrived within three to four minutes to find the baby being treated on a trolley.

‌



She said that both parents came into the room during the resuscitation, explaining that this is standard practice as it helps parents appreciate "everything that can be done is being done".

"I recall one dad [McGowan-Fazackerley] was quite subdued and stood to my right," she told the court. "The other dad [Varley] was very dramatic and more dramatic than I have seen parents previously - a bit chaotic, he wouldn't stand still and let people support him. He wouldn’t listen to what was being said."

Varley was initially shouting "don't let him die!", she told the court. She said: "He was saying don’t stop - I presume he meant resuscitation. He then said: "'I f***ing killed him,'" the court heard.

‌



View 4 Images Jamie Varley (left), 37, sits in the dock at Preston Crown Court alongside co-accused John McGowan-Fazakerley, 32 (Image: Elizabeth Cook/PA Wire)

When it was determined Preston could not be saved, and resuscitation efforts were stopped, she said Varley attempted to carry on CPR himself. She said she had to be "quite firm and tell him to stop what he was doing to Preston".

Nurse Rosanna Briggs told the jury she took an account from the family of what had happened to Preston. She was told Varley had left Preston in a bath seat while he went to get a towel and returned to find him drowning, the court heard.

‌



However, doctors noted that Preston was dry and that there was no water expelled from his lungs as would be expected. Blood gas tests suggested he had been without oxygen for longer than the 10 minutes reported, Dr Ram Patel said.

The court also heard a statement from a healthcare assistant who took the parents to an empty room while Preston was in resuscitation. She described Varley as "difficult to manage" as he continued to try and reach Preston.

She said: "At one point he even said 'all my fault' and 'can’t die'. He said 'I am a teacher. I am a year head. I have a level three in child protection.'"

‌



View 4 Images John McGowan-Fazackerley (Image: X)

The healthcare assistant later raised a number of concerns about her interactions with the couple. She said McGowan-Fazackerley gave inconsistent accounts, first saying he had gone into the house to find Jamie giving CPR and later saying he had been locked out because the keys were in the door.

She also noted that neither man was wearing shoes, which she found unusual, and that Preston’s nappy was dry. She added that Varley's comments about being a teacher with child protection training seemed odd given the circumstances.

Article continues below

Varley denies murder, manslaughter, two counts of assault by penetration, five counts of cruelty to a child, grievous bodily harm, sexual assault of a child, 13 counts of taking indecent photos or videos of a child, one count of distributing an indecent photo of a child to his co-accused and one count of making an indecent photo.

McGowan-Fazakerley denies allowing the death of a child, three counts of child cruelty and one count of sexual assault of a child. The trial continues.

News.title: Watch: Captain of stranded ship in Strait of Hormuz tells BBC of 'pressure'

News.title: FedEx driver sentenced to death by lethal injection for murder of seven-year-old in Texas
News.content:

A FedEx driver who admitted last month to the 2022 kidnapping and murder of seven-year-old Athena Strand has been sentenced to death.

Tanner Horner, 34, pleaded guilty to capital murder on April 7 at the start of his trial, immediately sending the case into the penalty phase.

A Texas jury reached its decision Tuesday after 19 days of testimony. The sentence will be automatically appealed to the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals.

Horner faced a punishment of either life in prison without parole or the death penalty. Prosecutors sought the death penalty, pointing to key evidence including a chilling, roughly hour-long audio recording captured inside Horner’s delivery van during the attack.

open image in gallery Tanner Lynn Horner was sentenced to death for the murder of Athena Strand ( AP )

The jury also heard testimony from investigators about Horner’s confession, the search for Athena, and the recovery of her body.

According to prosecutors, Horner was delivering packages to Athena’s home in Paradise, Texas, in November 2022 when he abducted her, placing her in his truck before killing her.

In closing arguments on May 5, Wise County District Attorney James Stainton said the case was among the “worst of the worst,” and the kind of situation the state reserves the death penalty for.

open image in gallery Horner was delivering packages to Athena’s home in Paradise, Texas, in November 2022 when he abducted her, placing her in his truck before killing her, prosecutors say ( Texas EQUUSEARCH )

Defense attorneys urged jurors to spare Horner’s life, presenting testimony about his troubled upbringing, autism diagnosis, exposure to toxic levels of lead, and mental health struggles.

They argued prosecutors failed to prove he would pose a continuing threat in prison and said those factors warranted a life sentence. But jurors rejected those arguments.

Emotions ran high in the courtroom as the sentence was read, with family members of Athena could be heard crying. Her uncle spoke to Horner directly, describing the lasting impact of her death on the family.

“You did not just take a life,” he said. “You destroyed a family. You took a little girl who trusted the world and repaid that innocence with violence. You chose to cause pain that will last generations. You say you found God, but what you did to Athena stands in direct opposition to everything that you now claim to believe.”

“You will face the wrath of God,” he continued. “I want you to know that you are nothing. You are a footnote in Athena's story. Her name will forever be remembered. Her name will forever be celebrated and everyone will forget you. You wanted your 15 minutes of fame. You got it. And no one's going to remember you after this.”

News.content:

Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday quoted '90s hip-hop party pioneers Cypress Hill to describe the Trump administration's view of Iran's remaining leadership amid a standoff over the Strait of Hormuz.

Speaking to reporters in the White House briefing room — as the first in what is understood to be a series of stand-ins for Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt while she is on maternity leave — Rubio said the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports would continue until Iran ceases efforts to prevent free maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz through what he described as “piracy.”

“There is no scenario here in which, if they decide to join a ladder of escalation, they wind up getting the last say, but our preference is for these straits to be opened to the way they're supposed to be open, back to the way it was. Anyone can use it. No mines in the water, nobody paying tolls. That's what we have to get back to, and that's the goal here,” he said.

“The time has come for Iran to make a sensible choice, and it's not easy for them to do that, obviously, because they have a fracture in their own leadership system ... and apart from that, I mean, the top people in that government are, to say the least ... they're insane in the brain, and so we need to address that.”

Rubio’s quip about the mental condition of leadership in Tehran was lifted straight from the chorus of “Insane in the Brain,” the first single off Cypress Hill’s 1993 album “Black Sunday.”

Rubio turned to Cypress Hill's 'Insane in the Brain' to describe the condition of Tehran's leaders ( AP )

Originally a diss track aimed at rival rappers Chubb Rock and Kid Frost, the hit song was described by The Independent’s then-music critic, Ben Thompson, as "potent dose of marijuana-inflected nasal squeak-rap” and “the party record of the aeon.”

He later reached back another year into the American hip-hop discography after telling reporters how Tehran is “facing real, catastrophic destruction to their economy, generational destruction to their economy, generational destruction to the wealth of their country imposed on themselves by the by the actions that they're taking.”

Quoting the N.W.A. rapper and actor Ice Cube’s 1992 song “Check Yo Self,” Rubio later added: “They should check themselves before they wreck themselves in the direction that they're going.”

The secretary of state, who also serves as President Donald Trump’s national security advisor, has long had a habit of inserting rap and hip-hop lyrics into his public remarks.

During a cabinet meeting in March, Rubio cribbed a line from Public Enemy’s 1990 single “Welcome to the Terrordome” when he said the Pentagon “lets the drummer get wicked over every portion of Iran that has military capabilities,” echoing Chuck D’s lyrics: “I got so much trouble on my mind/Refuse to lose/Here's your ticket/Hear the drummer get wicked.”

Earlier in the year, he cited Notorious BIG’s “Juicy” when discussing the U.S. operation to remove ex-Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro, telling reporters: “If you don’t know, now you know.”

Rubio is known to be a massive fan of Public Enemy, having told GQ in 2012 that the pioneering group was “transformative” in a way that had a huge influence on the East Coast and West Coast rap artists he listened to as a young man.

In addition to being the first person to serve as both Secretary of State and National Security Adviser, he is also known to have a longtime interest in spinning records and was recently filmed stepping into a DJ booth for a turn at a family wedding.

Asked what name he calls himself when behind the turntables, he declined to answer and told reporters: “You’re not ready for my DJ name.”

The ex-Florida senator’s turn at the White House lectern wasn’t the only Trump administration official’s outing before reporters that produced a strange moment.

Earlier in the day, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was forced to deny a claim that Iran has trained dolphins to conduct suicide attacks against U.S. forces and commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Speaking at a press briefing at the Pentagon alongside Joint Chiefs of Staff Chair General Dan Caine, Hegseth was asked about “reports of kamikaze dolphins” that have appeared in some news outlets after Iran claimed it could use previously unused weapons in the two-month-old conflict. The BBC reported in 2000 that Tehran once purchased dolphins that had been trained for military operations.

Caine at first looked incredulous and said, “I haven’t heard the kamikaze dolphins thing” before joking, ‘You mean like sharks with laser beams?” a reference to the 1997 film Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, in which Mike Myers’ character Dr. Evil complains that he could not acquire “sharks with frickin’ laser beams on their heads” and was forced to settle for laser-equipped “mutant sea bass.”

Hegseth then fielded the question, which appeared to emanate from an earlier Wall Street Journal report on Iran grasping for ways to break the Trump blockade of the strait.

“I can’t confirm or deny whether we have kamikaze dolphins, but I can confirm they [Iran] don’t,” Hegseth said.
